extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets and satirists; writers of verse seeking practical/style guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and stylistic precepts for composing satirical verse and poetry — covering tone, diction, revision, audience, and legal/moral risks. Advice is aimed at poets crafting durable, well-timed, and well-polished satires rather than ephemeral crowd-pleasers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness / Brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is need of conciseness that the sentence may run, and not embarrass itself with verbiage, that overloads the sated ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid superfluous words and long-winded sentences that tire the listener/reader. Keep lines and sentences flowing; cut verbiage that clogs the ear. Concision improves readability and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied tone and rhetorical control
rubrics_metrics.description: and sometimes a grave, frequently jocose style is necessary, supporting the character one while of the orator and [at another] of the poet, now and then that of a graceful rallier that curbs the force of his pleasantry and weakens it on purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switch tone deliberately (serious, jocose, oratorical, playful) to suit content and effect. Learn to modulate intensity—sometimes restrain pleasantry to achieve balance and rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ridicule as an instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: For ridicule often decides matters of importance more effectually and in a better manner, than severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ ridicule strategically: it can be more persuasive than harsh severity. Use satire to expose faults effectively, but pair it with judgement about when ridicule is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous mixing of foreign (Greek) words
rubrics_metrics.description: But [Lucilius, say they,] did a great thing, when he intermixed Greek words with Latin. O late-learned dunces!... When you make verses, I ask you this question; were you to undertake the difficult cause... would you... choose to intermix words borrowed from abroad, like the double-tongued Canusinian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with foreignisms or learned affectations. Mixing languages or exotic diction can seem ostentatious or inappropriate — prefer natural, fitting diction for the subject and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast and excessive ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: While bombastical Alpinus murders Memnon, and while he deforms the muddy source of the Rhine, I amuse myself with these satires;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of inflated, overwrought, or grandiose language where it does not suit the subject. Grandeur for its own sake can deform your work; prefer aptness and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness and finish of verse
rubrics_metrics.description: I did say, that the verses of Lucilius did not run smoothly... he would have retrenched a great deal from his writings: he would have pruned off every thing that transgressed the limits of perfection; and, in the composition of verses, would often have scratched his head, and bit his nails to the quick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish lines for metrical and rhetorical smoothness. Remove rough spots and inconsistencies; aim for finished, well-shaped verse rather than raw, episodic brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent revision / 'blot frequently'
rubrics_metrics.description: You that intend to write what is worthy to be read more than once, blot frequently:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise repeatedly. Do not be content with first drafts; editing and pruning are essential to produce work that endures and rewards re-reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for judicious/learned readers rather than mass applause
rubrics_metrics.description: take no-pains to make the multitude admire you, content with a few [judicious] readers. What, would you be such a fool as to be ambitious that your verses should be taught in petty schools? ... It is enough for me, that the knight [Maecenas] applauds:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the judgement of competent, learned readers and peers over popularity. Durable literary merit is more important than pleasing the uninformed crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance beyond mere laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Hence it is by no means sufficient to make an auditor grim with laughter: and yet there is some degree of merit even in this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write satire merely to provoke laughter; aim for depth and purpose. Humor should serve an intellectual or moral point, not be an end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject to personal ability and genre suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Desirous I am... to celebrate the achievements of the invincible Caesar, certain of bearing off ample rewards for your pains. Desirous I am... but my strength fails me... no verses of Horace's, unless well-timed, will gain the attention of Caesar;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects you are capable of handling well and that suit your style. Avoid ambitious themes (e.g., epic battle-scenes) unless you possess the skill and authority to treat them convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: no verses of Horace's, unless well-timed, will gain the attention of Caesar;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the right moment to publish or perform a piece. Even good work may fail if ill-timed; effectiveness depends on context and opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scandalous personal invective and be mindful of legal/social risk
rubrics_metrics.description: be sure of this if any person shall make scandalous verses against a particular man, an action lies, and a sentence. Granted, if they are scandalous: but if a man composes good ones, and is praised by such a judge as Caesar?... If a man barks only at him who deserves his invectives, while he himself is unblamable? The process will be canceled with laughter:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use satire to launch baseless, scandalous attacks on individuals — there are legal and social consequences. Ensure your targets deserve criticism and that you are not guilty of comparable fault.
